I don't recall a specific replication attempt of it, though it may have been included in a larger replication project. Many cultural psychology studies have a mixed replication record, but I can't tie an outcome to this one.

Sheppes et al. (2011), "Emotion-Regulation Choice," found that people choose distraction over reappraisal when emotional intensity is high, and reappraisal when it is low. I recall this finding being replicated in follow-up work, including Sheppes et al. 2014 and several others. I do not specifically recall a formal replication project that targeted this exact study, though it may have been included in a large-scale effort. My recollection of a registered replication outcome is therefore weak.

I do recall a replication of the broader idea: a Many Labs-style or Registered Replication project tested the action/inaction priming effect. I can't pin down its outcome, and I don't recall a specific replication of this exact paper. The related literature on goal priming has replicated poorly in general.

It was a laboratory experiment on job design, with principals choosing between "good" jobs (discretion) and "bad" jobs, and I can't point to a replication of it, whether in the Many Labs-style projects or the Camerer et al. 2016 economics replication project. Kidd & Castano (2013) was replicated by Panero et al. (2016), which reported failures to replicate across multiple experiments. The Many Labs 2 project also tested it, and I believe it did not replicate there either. The replication outcome is therefore a failure.

```json

Lee & Schwarz (2010) is the "washing away postdecisional dissonance" study. It was part of the Many Labs-style replication efforts. Specifically, Earp, Everett, Madva, & Hamlin (2014) tried to replicate the Schnall-style cleansing effects, and Fayard et al. (2009) was an earlier related replication. Separately, Camerer et al. (2018), the Social Science Replication Project, did not include this study. Johnson, Cheung, & Donnellan (2014) replicated Schnall et al. 2008 rather than Lee & Schwarz. Gámez et al. (2011) was a Spanish replication of the Lee & Schwarz study. The Open Science Collaboration's Reproducibility Project: Psychology also did not include it, as far as I recall.

I do recall that Lee & Schwarz's work was replicated in a registered report of a Many Labs-type effort (Lee, Schwarz et al.), but I am not certain of the details. I do recall one failure: Camerer et al. did not cover it, but a Kaspar (2013) replication found no effect.

On balance I recognize the study, and I believe the replication outcome was a failure.

```json
{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "failure", "confidence": 0.5}
```

The study is Rand, Greene & Nowak (2012), which argued that intuitive, fast decisions favor cooperation. I do recall replication attempts. Bouwmeester et al. (2017) ran a registered replication report across 21 labs and found no overall effect of time pressure on cooperation. Some other work, such as Rand's own re-analyses, found effects only among participants who understood the task. The Many Labs-style attempts mostly failed, so the outcome is failure or mixed. I lean toward failure.

```json

```

I recognize this study. Shah, Mullainathan, & Shafir (2012) is the scarcity paper, with experiments on Family Feud-style games, where poor participants borrowed more and performed worse. I recall that the Many Labs-style or other replication attempts, such as the Camerer-style large-scale replication, did not produce a clear result. Replications of related scarcity work (e.g., Mani et al. 2013) have had mixed results. I can't pin down a specific replication of this exact paper, though one may exist in the SCORE project.

{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "mixed", "confidence": 0.3}

This is a ego depletion study (Schmeichel, 2007). It may have been included in a replication project, possibly the Many Labs or a Registered Replication Report, but I don't recall a specific replication of this exact paper. Ego depletion replications in general, such as Hagger et al. 2016, tended to fail, but that RRR used a different paradigm.

{"recognized_study": false, "recalled_replication_outcome": "none", "confidence": 0.3}

The Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) anchoring study was replicated in Many Labs 1 (Klein et al., 2014), which used the same high and low anchors for estimates such as the population of Chicago and the height of Mt. Everest. The anchoring effect replicated very robustly there, and with large effect sizes.

{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "success", "confidence": 0.9}

Bargh & Shalev (2012) reported that loneliness correlates with taking warmer showers and baths. I recall a replication: Donnellan, Lucas, and Cesario (2015), "On the association between loneliness and bathing habits: Nine replications of Bargh and Shalev (2012) Study 1," Emotion. They ran nine replications, all with larger samples, and found effects that were small and mostly nonsignificant, with a pooled estimate near r = .04 or so. That counts as a failure. Hxxx also, Many Labs-type efforts on the related warmth-priming work. So I recognize the study and recall a failure.

```json
{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "failure", "confidence": 0.85}

I recall this study. It is a money-priming paper, and money priming is a well-known target of failed replications. Rohrer, Pashler, and Harris (2015) failed to replicate Caruso et al.'s related money-priming findings on system justification, and the Many Labs 3 project did not replicate the 2013 study either. The 2013 paper is also the one linked to the Caruso, Vohs, Baxter, and Waytz experiments on endorsement of free-market systems. The most likely outcome is a failure.

```json

The study is Knobe's "Chairman" or "side-effect effect" experiment: harm vs. help conditions, with people more likely to say the chairman intentionally harmed the environment than that he intentionally helped it.

I do recall replications of this effect. It is a robust finding that has been replicated many times, including in cross-cultural work and in the Many Labs-style X-Phi Replicability Project (Cova et al., 2018), where the Knobe effect replicated. So I would call the outcome a success.

```json
{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "success", "confidence": 0.9}
```

This is the disfluency study, which showed that hard-to-read fonts improved performance on the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT). I recall replication attempts. Thompson et al. (2013) and Meyer et al. (2015, "Disfluent fonts don't help people solve math problems," JEP:G) failed to replicate the effect. Many-labs-style work and a meta-analysis (Xie et al., 2019) also found little or no effect. The Meyer et al. paper reported failures across 16 studies with a large combined sample.

In the SCORE or other replication project context, the replication was probably a failure.

```json
{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "failure", "confidence": 0.85}
```

I don't specifically recall a replication attempt of it, so I can't say how one turned out. There may be conceptual replications of sound symbolism in brand names, but I can't tie any to this paper with confidence.

I recognize the study: McKinstry, Dale & Spivey (2008) used mouse-tracking to show that number comparison, such as 3 vs 5 against 2 vs 5, produces curved trajectories that reflect parallel competition. I don't recall a specific replication of it, though the broader mouse-tracking literature has replicated similar effects. I can't confirm any replication outcome for this exact study.

This is Williams & Bargh (2008), "Keeping One's Distance: The Influence of Spatial Distance Cues on Affect and Evaluation." Participants plotted points on a Cartesian plane, which primed psychological distance and changed their ratings of emotional attachment to family and their evaluations of various stimuli.

I recall that it was included in the Many Labs 3 replication project (Ebersole et al., 2016), and that a separate replication was done by Pashler, Rohrer, and Harris on a related "Warmth" study (Williams & Bargh 2008, Science), which is a different paper. For this paper, the Psychological Science distance priming study, I believe Pashler et al. (2013) also failed to replicate its results. Together, the evidence points to replication failures.

```json
{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "failure", "confidence": 0.7}
```

Bressan & Stranieri (2008) reported that women in a relationship rate single men as less attractive, while partnered women rate committed men as more attractive. Women who were partnered and not in the fertile phase, in particular, were more attracted to taken men. The claim is that "mate-choice copying" is moderated by relationship status and hormonal contraceptive use.

I recall that the study was used in the Many Labs-style or Psychological Science replication contexts, but I cannot identify a specific replication with confidence. There is a known replication-style work on mate-choice copying (e.g., Hill & Buss 2008, and later studies by Jones et al.), and some of these found mixed results. Nothing definitive comes to mind for this exact paper.

It may have been included in a large-scale replication project, but I can't recall an outcome, so I'm not claiming one.

I recall that its sample sizes were small and that the effect was subtle. I don't recall a specific replication of it, though it may have been included in a larger replication project.

Marcora et al. (2009) is a well-known study showing that mental fatigue (90 minutes of AX-CPT) reduced time to exhaustion in cycling. It is the original paper behind the psychobiological model of endurance performance.

Several related replications and extensions exist, such as Pageaux et al. 2013, 2014, and Brown & Bray, plus meta-analyses on mental fatigue and physical performance. Many of these found similar effects, though some failed to replicate. I can't point to one direct, formal replication of this specific study. It was not part of a major replication project that I know of, though it could have been included in a recent multi-lab effort.

Because I only recall conceptual replications and meta-analyses, not a specific direct replication, I'm leaning toward "none" or "mixed".

```json
{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "mixed", "confidence": 0.3}

Southgate, Senju & Csibra (2007) is the anticipatory looking false-belief study with 2-year-olds. I recall replication attempts, but they are mixed. Kulke et al. (2018) failed to replicate anticipatory looking in a similar paradigm. Schuwerk et al. also had difficulty, and the ManyBabies 2 project addressed this. I can't pin down a replication of this specific study with a clear outcome. Overall the recalled evidence leans toward failure or mixed.

```json
{"recognized_study": true, "recalled_replication_outcome": "mixed", "confidence": 0.5}

Greene et al. (2008) is a well-known study, and I do recall replication attempts of it. Most notably, Many Labs-type and independent efforts, including Tinghög et al. (2016, "Cognitive load selectively interferes with utilitarian moral judgment: a replication study"), tested the claim and did not find the effect. Tinghög et al. found no significant effect of cognitive load on utilitarian judgments, and the original reaction-time interaction did not replicate either. This was a failure to replicate.

I recognize this study. It is the Marcus et al. (1999) finding that 7-month-olds generalize ABA/ABB rule patterns after short familiarization. Replications exist. Some were successful, such as Marcus's own follow-ups and the Many Babies-style work on related phenomena. Others were mixed or failed. Rabagliati, Ferguson, and Lew-Williams (2019) reviewed the evidence on rule learning in infants and found it weaker than assumed. Some labs failed to replicate with the original stimuli, and the Many Babies group reported variable results. Overall my recollection is mixed.

```json

I do recall replication attempts of this study. The "brain drain" effect has been tested several times, and the results were largely unfavorable. Examples include Ruiz Pardo & Minda (2022), Schwaiger & Tahir (2020), and Hartmann and colleagues, and several of them found no significant effect of smartphone presence on cognitive capacity. A few studies reported small or conditional effects, but the overall picture is that the original finding did not replicate well. I am not certain which specific replication is the one this question refers to, so my confidence is moderate.

```json

I don't recall a specific replication of it, though the effect belongs to a family of studies on generic masculine effects that other researchers have replicated or extended. That makes it plausible, but I can't point to a replication outcome for this study itself.

Yes, I recognize this study. Carter, Ferguson & Hassin (2011) reported that a single exposure to the American flag shifted political attitudes toward Republicanism. It is a well-known flag priming study. Its replication history includes Klein et al.'s Many Labs 4 (or Many Labs 1, which tested flag priming and found no effect on conservatism, from Carter et al.'s original flag prime study). Many Labs 1 (Klein et al., 2014) replicated Carter et al. 2011 and found no significant effect. This was a failure to replicate. Within the SCORE/Replication project, the outcome would also be a failure.

```json

The study is a classic terror management theory paper. It argues that mortality salience effects emerge after a delay, when death-related thoughts are highly accessible but outside conscious attention. I do not recall a specific replication of this exact study. The nearest large-scale effort is the Many Labs 4 mortality salience replication, which tested a different original (Greenberg et al., 1994, study 1: the American-participants-and-pro/anti-American-essay paradigm). It found no significant effect. That makes the Many Labs 4 project plausibly the replication attempt for this reference, with a failure outcome. The Many Labs 4 target was Study 1 of Greenberg et al. (1994), which is this paper, but I am not certain of the match.

```json
